docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

Known limits of exo-v2v 0.6.0. exo-v2v plan reports the ones it can detect before anything is created.

docs.title: Source VM
docs.text: Limit Details At most 5 data disks as volumes An Exoscale instance attaches up to 5 Block Storage volumes next to its root disk. Disks carried inside the root disk (--fold, automatic for a disk that shares a filesystem with the system disk) do not count. A volume rebuild at cutover needs a free slot per rebuilt volume. System disk Found from the boot order or VMware Tools; plan warns when it had to guess (run it with the VM on and Tools running, or pass --system-disk) Snapshot chains Supported. A revert to a snapshot during replication makes the next cycle a full copy of the allocated areas Disk changes during replication A grown disk is followed (volume resized; a grown system disk resets the target instance, whose root disk is then copied again), a new disk gets a new volume, a removed disk stops sync Windows dynamic disks and Storage Spaces Not supported on data disks: their metadata counts 512-byte sectors. The disks are detected and left untouched; their volumes stay unreadable on Exoscale. Convert them to basic disks first (a spanned or striped volume must be copied to a basic volume). plan warns when VMware Tools show a volume spread over several disks. No independent disks or RDMs Independent disks are left out of snapshots, so changes cannot be tracked. Raw device mappings are not VMDK files. Root disk of 10 GB or more Smaller disks are rounded up to 10 GB Disk sizes rounded up Each disk becomes the next whole GB; volumes get at least 1 MiB extra Network interfaces A single migration gets one public interface (DHCP). In a group, each port group maps to the public interface or a managed private network, and the guest's configuration follows. Static IP addresses In a group, a static address on a private port group is kept on the Exoscale private network. Otherwise the guest keeps its old static configuration: switch it to DHCP before the cutover, or update it on the instance. Secure Boot and vTPM Carried over: the instance is created with Secure Boot and a TPM when the source has them (Exoscale sets both at creation). Secrets sealed to the VMware vTPM do not move. Secure Boot is tested; the TPM is not. A guest that only boots because Secure Boot is off at the source cannot gain it later: Exoscale cannot turn it on after creation. Encrypted disks and encrypted VMs Not supported (LUKS, BitLocker, vSphere VM encryption)

docs.title: Block Storage sector size
docs.text:
Exoscale Block Storage volumes use 4096-byte sectors; VMware disks use 512. exo-v2v adapts data volumes at cutover, with these limits:

Case Behaviour Partition tables (GPT, MBR) Rewritten in place. Partitions must start on a 4 KiB boundary, which is the default for every current installer. NTFS (Windows) Adapted in place, no data moved. The volume must use clusters of 4 KiB or more (the default). XFS created with 512-byte sectors (RHEL-family default on VMware), ext with 1 KiB blocks Rebuilt on a new volume with the same identifiers. The cutover takes longer in proportion to the data on these volumes. The original volume is kept, detached, as a rollback copy until cleanup --delete-rollback-volumes. The same filesystems inside LVM logical volumes Rebuilt the same way, logical volume by logical volume. A volume group spread over several volumes is rebuilt across as many new volumes, keeping the PV, VG and LV identifiers. Linear and striped logical volumes only: thin, RAID, mirror, cache and snapshot logical volumes with such a filesystem are reported, not rebuilt. A volume group that spans the system disk and other disks Those disks are carried inside the root disk (512-byte sectors), so nothing is rebuilt. Detected by plan through VMware Tools; otherwise the preflight at the first sync reports it: plan again with --fold DISK. Root disk Not affected: the instance's root disk uses 512-byte sectors

docs.title: Replication
docs.text: Limit Details The appliance must run in the source vSphere It reads snapshot disks by attaching them to itself, so it must be on a host that sees the VM's datastores. Copy speed Limited by the datastore and the appliance's CPU. In our lab (HDD datastore) a full copy ran at 7–38 MiB/s per VM, about 60 MiB/s for a 4 vCPU appliance copying 5 VMs at once (sizing). Later cycles copy only changes. Snapshot per cycle Each cycle creates and removes a snapshot, which briefly pauses the VM, as backups do Target instance restarts during replication The target instance runs its agent from memory and keeps the boot sectors of the system disk off the disk until the conversion: if it restarts, nothing boots. Run exo-v2v recover NAME: the next sync copies the system disk again, and the volumes only for their changes. Egress of the target instance None until the cutover (receiver templates): its security group gets a rule that matches nothing. The cutover removes it before it stops the source; the IAM role needs delete-rule-from-security-group (0.4.1). Instance type during replication The target instance runs as standard.large or larger until the cutover, then is scaled to its final type Datastore types Tested on VMFS. vSAN and vVols are untested. vCenter Tested against govmomi's vCenter simulator only: vMotion, Storage vMotion and DRS moves during a replication, and privilege enforcement, are untested on a real vCenter (vCenter). The appliance's host must mount every datastore of the VMs it replicates

docs.title: Cutover and after
docs.text: Limit Details Downtime Shutdown, last delta, conversion (2–5 min) and boot: 2 to 9 minutes in our tests, longer if a volume must be rebuilt Rollback exo-v2v rollback powers the source VM back on. Data written on Exoscale after the cutover is not copied back. Windows first boot Windows finishes installing drivers for a few minutes after RDP opens and may reboot. Data disks come online when it finishes. Windows licensing Contact Exoscale before migrating Windows workloads (see Supported operating systems) Zones Tested in ch-gva-2. Conversion needs nested virtualization on the instance type.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text: Limit Details One appliance per group It replicates every member, so it must see all their datastores Selecting members group discover --vm (name or inventory path), --folder, --tag (vCenter): see vCenter One zone Every member of a group goes to the same zone Private networks Managed private networks only (no VPC subnets). The top host address of the subnet (.254 of a /24) belongs to Exoscale's DHCP server: a VM using it must be renumbered. The appliance role only attaches v2v-* private networks Default route Moves to the public interface: a private network has no router. Routes to other networks through the old gateway are lost DNS servers Static DNS servers in the guests' configurations are kept; change on-premises ones before or during the cutover (post_cutover hook) Elastic IPs Manual Elastic IPs (Public IPs and DNS); managed (health-checked) Elastic IPs are not handled DNS Only A records of Exoscale DNS zones are switched; other providers: the post_cutover hook Health checks Run from the appliance against the members' public IPs (the ports are opened to the appliance only) Rollback after conversion Converted members must be created again before another attempt (a full copy)

docs.title: Rehearsal
docs.text: Limit Details Receiver templates A rehearsal needs receiver templates built with exo-v2v 0.4 or later (copies without a public IP read their metadata from a drive, not from the metadata server) Consistency Each copy is crash-consistent at its own seed time. group rehearse --consistent puts every member at one point (snapshots within 13 s for 5 VMs in our lab, 44 s quiesced); vSphere has no snapshot across VMs, so "one point" is within the spread the report shows What it cannot test The public side (public IP, DNS switch, security groups on the public interface) and anything that needs the internet or on-premises systems: those fail by design; the report lists the names the copies tried to resolve Windows Activation and domain servers are unreachable unless they are members of the group Metadata drive The copies see a small extra disk (1 MiB) as their second disk: mount data disks by UUID or label, not by device name Windows copies Crash-consistent NTFS: the copy's system volume journal is reset before conversion and checked by Windows at first boot Cost One instance per copy plus the relay, and the copies' volumes, for the rehearsal's lifetime (TTL 8 h by default with exo-v2v gc)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

Check these before your first migration. exo-v2v plan checks the source VM for you and refuses VMs it cannot migrate.

docs.title: vSphere
docs.text:
Item Requirement Version vCenter Server (roles, folders, tags, DRS) or standalone ESXi, 6.7 or later. Tested on ESXi 7.0 Update 3; vCenter against its simulator. Account A vSphere account with the privileges below, passed to exo-v2v as VSPHERE_HOST, VSPHERE_USER and VSPHERE_PASSWORD Datastore space Room for a short-lived snapshot of each VM during each sync cycle (the changes written while a cycle runs)

Privileges for the migration account:

On Privileges Source VMs VirtualMachine.State.CreateSnapshot, VirtualMachine.State.RemoveSnapshot, VirtualMachine.Config.ChangeTracking, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOff, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOn, VirtualMachine.Provisioning.DiskRandomRead Replication appliance VM VirtualMachine.Config.AddExistingDisk, VirtualMachine.Config.RemoveDisk Datastores of the source VMs Datastore.FileManagement (read)

docs.title: Replication appliance
docs.text:
The appliance is a Linux VM that runs exo-v2v. It must run inside the same vSphere environment as the VMs you migrate, on a host that can see their datastores: exo-v2v attaches the frozen snapshot disks to it read-only. One appliance can serve many migrations.

Item Requirement Operating system Ubuntu 24.04 or Debian 12 or later (any Linux with Python 3.10+ works) Size 2 vCPU, 4 GiB RAM, 20 GB disk. Copy throughput is limited by the appliance's CPU; give it 4 vCPU for several migrations in parallel. SCSI controller A VMware Paravirtual (pvscsi) controller with free slots, used to attach the snapshot disks. Add a second one if you run many migrations at once. Software Python 3.10 or later, ssh, the exo CLI 1.102 or later, and exo-v2v (pip install exo_v2v-*.whl); systemd for unattended replication Privileges sync, cutover and rollback read block devices and must run as root (sudo -E keeps the environment variables)

Network access from the appliance:

Destination Port Why vCenter or ESXi TCP 443 vSphere API Exoscale API (api-<zone>.exoscale.com) TCP 443 Create and manage the target instance Target instances in the Exoscale zone TCP 22 Data stream and agent control, inside SSH api.ipify.org or ifconfig.me TCP 443 Detects the appliance's public address once per migration. Not needed if you pass create --sender-cidr. A rehearsal's relay (rehearsals only) TCP 22 The appliance drives the copies through it; the production receivers stream the root disks through it Group members' public IPs (groups only) the health check ports group cutover checks each tier from the appliance; the member's own security group opens those ports to the appliance only Your alert webhook (optional) TCP 443 Alerts

The appliance's public address must stay the same during a migration: the migration's security group admits SSH from that address only.

The web status page listens on the appliance's loopback interface by default; reach it through an SSH port forward.

docs.title: Exoscale
docs.text: Item Requirement Account An organization with quota for the instance types you target, Block Storage volumes and one security group per running migration; for a group, one private network per private port group and every member's receiver at once API key A key restricted to the Compute service, configured in the exo CLI (exo config) or in EXOSCALE_API_KEY and EXOSCALE_API_SECRET. See IAM role for a ready-made role. Instance type during migration Conversion needs at least 8 GiB of RAM and nested virtualization, so the target instance runs as standard.large (or larger) until cutover, then is scaled to its final type. Tested in ch-gva-2. Internet access from the target instance Not needed with a receiver template. Without one, the target instance installs packages from Debian or Ubuntu mirrors, and for Windows guests downloads the virtio drivers from fedorapeople.org.

docs.title: Source VM
docs.text: Item Requirement Operating system See Supported operating systems Disks At most 6 virtual disks (1 root disk and up to 5 Block Storage volumes). No independent disks, no raw device mappings (RDM). Firmware BIOS or UEFI. The target instance uses the same boot mode, and Secure Boot and a TPM when the source has them. Changed Block Tracking Enabled automatically by exo-v2v, without downtime VMware Tools Recommended, running when you run plan: it tells exo-v2v which disk holds the system and which disks share a filesystem with it. At cutover it shuts the guest down cleanly; without it, exo-v2v powers the VM off after --shutdown-timeout. Network configuration For a single migration, DHCP is recommended: a static IP configuration keeps the old address and must be updated for the Exoscale instance's address. In a group, static addresses on private port groups are kept on Exoscale private networks. Snapshots Existing snapshots are allowed but consolidate them first if you can

docs.title: Public IPs and DNS
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

A migrated VM gets a new public address on Exoscale. exo-v2v handles what follows from that: an Elastic IP known before the window, the reverse DNS name (mail servers), the DNS records that point at the service, and private addresses that must change.

Need How A public address known in advance, that outlives the instance An Elastic IP, reserved at create, attached at cutover, configured in the guest A PTR record (mail servers, some partners) Reverse DNS on the Elastic IP or the instance, set at create Names pointed at the new address at the right time DNS records on Exoscale DNS: TTL lowered at create, switched once the instance is healthy, put back by rollback A private address that cannot stay (the .254 Exoscale keeps, a subnet that overlaps) Renumbering: a new address per VM, or a whole network moved to a new range Firewall rules that name other groups Security group rules with sg:NAME sources

docs.title: Elastic IPs
docs.text:
exo-v2v plan web01 --vm web01 --zone ch-gva-2 --elastic-ip new --reverse-dns www.example.com

In a group manifest:

vms:
  - vm: lb01
    public: {elastic_ip: new, reverse_dns: shop.example.com}
  - vm: mail01
    public: {elastic_ip: 194.182.10.20}      # an Elastic IP you already have, in the same zone
Step What happens create new reserves an Elastic IP (description v2v-<migration>); an address you give must exist in the zone and be free. The address is printed: tell partners, update firewalls and DNS ahead cutover The Elastic IP is attached to the stopped instance before it starts. The conversion configures it in the guest (below). The cutover waits for the instance's SSH or RDP port on the Elastic IP too; in a group, a member whose Elastic IP does not answer fails its health check rollback The source VM runs again with its old address; the Elastic IP stays reserved cleanup The Elastic IP stays: it is the production address. cleanup --delete-elastic-ips (or group cleanup --delete-elastic-ips) releases the ones exo-v2v reserved; an address you brought is never released

In the guest. Exoscale delivers an Elastic IP's traffic to the instance; the guest must hold the address:

  • Linux: v2v-eip.service puts every address of /etc/v2v-eip.list on the loopback interface at each boot (Exoscale's documented method). Replies leave from the Elastic IP; connections the guest opens still leave from the instance's own address.
  • Windows: Windows adds no address to an interface on DHCP, so a first-boot task turns the public NIC static with what its DHCP lease gave (address, gateway, DNS servers: an Exoscale instance keeps its public address) and adds the Elastic IP as a /32 that is never used as a source. If a step fails, DHCP comes back and the task tries again. Log: C:\ProgramData\exo-v2v\elastic-ip.log.

The instance keeps its own public address as well (health checks use it), and its security groups apply to the traffic of both addresses.

docs.title: Reverse DNS
docs.text: --reverse-dns NAME (or public.reverse_dns) sets the PTR record of the Elastic IP, or of the instance's address without one, at create. A mail server can then send from its final address the day it moves. The forward record (NAME → the address) is yours to create, or exo-v2v switches it (below).

docs.title: DNS records
docs.text:
For zones hosted on Exoscale DNS:

exo-v2v plan web01 --vm web01 --zone ch-gva-2 --dns-record www.example.com --dns-record example.com

dns:
  ttl: 60                                   # until cleanup
  records:
    www.example.com: lb01                   # A record -> lb01's Elastic IP (or its instance IP)
    example.com: lb01
Step What happens plan Each name must be one A record in a domain of the account (the longest matching domain holds it) create The current value and TTL of each record are saved, the TTL lowered to ttl. Wait at least the old TTL, plus two minutes, before the cutover: resolvers keep the old answer that long (the cutover warns otherwise) cutover Once the instance answers (a group: once the last tier is healthy, before post_cutover), each record points at the new address: the Elastic IP, or the instance's address. Then the zone's nameservers are asked until every one of their addresses answers the new address 10 times in a row (at most 3 minutes; the cutover never fails on it, and a group's window does not include it). A cutover whose instance did not answer leaves DNS alone: run exo-v2v cutover NAME again once it does rollback The old values back (the TTL stays low) cleanup The original TTL back

status and the web page show each record (old value, switched, how long until the nameservers served it, restored).

Exoscale's nameservers serve a change after a few seconds to about a minute (1 to 62 s in our tests). During that time each nameserver address can answer the old and the new value in turn, so a single dig that shows the new address does not mean the change is everywhere. The check runs from the appliance over UDP port 53; where that is blocked it logs that it could not check, and carries on. Only A records of Exoscale DNS zones are handled; for another DNS provider, switch them in the group's post_cutover hook ({lb01.address} is the Elastic IP or the instance address).

docs.title: Renumbering private addresses
docs.text:
A group keeps its VMs' private addresses by default. To change them:

networks:
  app:
    source: pg-app
    type: private
    cidr: 10.20.0.0/24
    renumber: 10.30.0.0/24          # every member keeps its host part: 10.20.0.31 -> 10.30.0.31

vms:
  - vm: db01
    ip: {app: 10.20.0.50}           # or one VM: its new address on that network

plan prints renumbered: OLD -> NEW. At the conversion, the guest's network configuration is rewritten in place wherever it names the old address (ifupdown, netplan, NetworkManager, ifcfg, systemd-networkd, and the guest's own line in /etc/hosts); Windows gets the new static address. Addresses inside applications (a database address in a configuration file, another VM's line in /etc/hosts) are not changed: renumber what nothing else names, or update those with a hook. renumber needs the same prefix length (host parts are kept); the .254 of a /24 still belongs to Exoscale's DHCP server.

docs.title: Security group rules
docs.text:
The rules of a manifest's security_groups take a CIDR or another security group as source:

security_groups:
  v2v-shop-db: ["tcp/5432 sg:v2v-shop-app", "icmp 10.20.0.0/24"]
  v2v-shop-app: ["tcp/8080 sg:v2v-shop-web"]

group create creates the groups that do not exist, with their rules, and keeps the rules of the groups it created in line with the manifest. For a security group that existed before, group plan shows the rules that differ and group create --update-rules adds the missing ones (it never removes rules from a group exo-v2v did not create).

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: The IAM role needs the Elastic IP operations (on v2v-* Elastic IPs: an existing address you bring needs a description starting with v2v-, or a rule of your own), the instance's reverse DNS, and, for DNS records, the dns service rule. These rules are in the policy file since 0.6.0.

docs.title: Receiver templates
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

A receiver template is an Exoscale template that boots straight into the exo-v2v receiver: a Linux system that runs entirely from RAM, so the migration can overwrite the instance's own disk. With a receiver template, exo-v2v create takes about one minute instead of 5 to 15, and the target instance needs no access to package mirrors.

Without one, create starts the target instance from a stock Linux template, installs the conversion tools on it and switches it into RAM (kexec). Both ways produce the same receiver; the rest of the migration is identical.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
Exoscale does not publish receiver templates yet: build and register your own (below). Exoscale-published Windows variants would carry the Windows licence, so a migrated Windows guest would run on a Windows-licensed instance. Until then, contact Exoscale about licensing before migrating Windows guests.

Templates built before exo-v2v 0.4.0 cannot serve a rehearsal: a copy has no public IP, and Exoscale then delivers the instance's metadata (the migration's SSH key) on a small read-only NoCloud drive instead of the metadata server; 0.4.0 templates read either. Rebuild them to rehearse.

Templates built before exo-v2v 0.2.0 lack dmsetup, which 0.2.0 uses to rebuild LVM logical volumes. Such a receiver installs it when it needs it, which requires access to a package mirror: rebuild your templates to avoid that.

docs.title: Variants
docs.text:
The template's boot mode must match the VM's firmware. One image boots in both modes, with or without Secure Boot (Canonical-signed shim, GRUB and kernel), so Secure Boot is chosen per instance, not per template.

Template Boot mode For exo-v2v-linux-uefi UEFI Linux VMs with UEFI firmware exo-v2v-linux-legacy legacy Linux VMs with BIOS firmware exo-v2v-windows-uefi UEFI Windows VMs with UEFI firmware exo-v2v-windows-legacy legacy Windows VMs with BIOS firmware

The Windows variants also carry the virtio-win drivers and rhsrvany that virt-v2v needs to convert Windows guests. A Windows VM with BIOS firmware keeps BIOS on Exoscale: no conversion to UEFI is needed.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
exo-v2v plan web01 --vm web01 --zone ch-gva-2 \
  --receiver-template exo-v2v-linux-uefi [--receiver-template-visibility private]
exo-v2v create web01

plan refuses a template whose boot mode does not match the VM. The receiver logs in as v2v; exo-v2v handles that.

docs.title: Build and register
docs.text:
template/receiver.pkr.hcl builds the image and registers both boot-mode variants with Exoscale's Packer plugin. Run it on Ubuntu 24.04, as a user with passwordless sudo, with an Exoscale API key that can register templates and write to an existing Object Storage bucket:

sudo apt-get install -y mmdebstrap qemu-utils gdisk dosfstools grub-pc-bin grub-efi-amd64-signed shim-signed
export EXOSCALE_API_KEY=EXO… EXOSCALE_API_SECRET=…
packer init template/
packer build -var flavour=linux   -var image_bucket=BUCKET template/   # exo-v2v-linux-uefi, -legacy
packer build -var flavour=windows -var image_bucket=BUCKET template/   # exo-v2v-windows-uefi, -legacy
Variable Default Meaning flavour linux linux, or windows (adds virtio-win and rhsrvany) image_bucket Existing bucket in the first zone; the image is removed after import zones ["ch-gva-2"] Zones to register the templates in (templates are per zone) template_prefix exo-v2v Template names: <prefix>-<flavour>-uefi and -legacy

The recipe runs template/build-image.sh, which you can also run by hand and register yourself:

sudo template/build-image.sh linux exo-v2v-linux.qcow2       # ~230 MB; windows: ~600 MB
exo storage upload exo-v2v-linux.qcow2 sos://BUCKET/
URL=$(exo storage presign sos://BUCKET/exo-v2v-linux.qcow2 -e 1h)
for m in uefi legacy; do
  exo compute instance-template register exo-v2v-linux-$m "$URL" "$(md5sum < exo-v2v-linux.qcow2 | cut -d' ' -f1)" \
    --zone ch-gva-2 --boot-mode $m --username v2v --disable-password
done

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The image is a 10 GB disk with a BIOS boot partition and an EFI system partition. GRUB loads the kernel and a ~220 MB initramfs that holds the whole receiver system (virt-v2v, libguestfs, QEMU, filesystem tools). The disk is never mounted.
  • At boot the receiver reads the migration's SSH key from the instance user-data, generates its own SSH host keys and starts SSH. The Windows variant first copies virtio-win from the EFI partition into RAM.
  • create waits for SSH before attaching the Block Storage volumes, then streams the exo-v2v agent over SSH and starts it.

docs.title: Rehearsal
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

A rehearsal starts copies of the migrated VMs on Exoscale, converted exactly as the cutover would convert them, so that you can check the application before the real move. The copies are airgapped: they cannot reach the sources, the production networks, your on-premises systems or the internet, so a copy of an application server never writes to the real database, sends mail or calls an API. People reach them only through a relay. The sources keep running and replication goes on; rehearse as often as you need, then throw the copies away.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text: Copies Every VM (or the members you pick) as an Exoscale instance with no public IP, seeded from its replica, converted by the cutover's own code, started in the cutover's tier order Checks The group's health checks, run on the relay against the copies Access SSH through the relay: shells on the copies, port forwards for web front ends and RDP. exo-v2v rehearsal connect prints the SSH configuration Report Seed, conversion and boot times per copy; a predicted cutover window; the names the copies tried to resolve (their outside dependencies: they all fail in the airgap, the report lists them) Lifetime Destroyed with one command, or by exo-v2v gc after its TTL (8 hours by default)

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
sudo -E exo-v2v group rehearse shop               # every member (or --vm db01 --vm app01)
sudo -E exo-v2v rehearse web01 --tcp 22           # a single migration, with a TCP health check
exo-v2v rehearsal status  shop
exo-v2v rehearsal connect shop                    # ssh config for the copies
exo-v2v rehearsal connect shop --forward lb01:80  # 127.0.0.1:10080 on the appliance -> the copy
exo-v2v rehearsal report  shop                    # refreshes the DNS log
exo-v2v rehearsal destroy shop
exo-v2v gc                                        # run hourly from cron: destroys expired rehearsals

docs.title: One point in time (--consistent)
docs.text:
By default each copy is seeded from its migration's last cycle, so members seeded minutes apart do not show one instant (an order in the application database that its server copy does not know yet). --consistent brings every member's replica to the same point first:

sudo -E exo-v2v group rehearse shop --consistent --quiesce      # --max-spread 30s fails above that
  1. Every member's migration is locked (no timer or other sync moves a replica on).
  2. A normal catch-up cycle runs, so the next snapshots hold little.
  3. One snapshot per member, all requested before any is waited for; vCenter's task times give the spread (first start to last completion). In our lab, for 5 VMs including a Windows server: 13 s, and 44 s with --quiesce (most of it Windows VSS). The report shows when each member's snapshot ended.
  4. Each member copies from its snapshot, then its copy is seeded before the lock is released.

--quiesce asks VMware Tools to quiesce each VM (VSS on Windows, the freeze scripts and fsfreeze on Linux): each copy is then application-consistent on its own. A VM that cannot quiesce gets a crash-consistent snapshot and the report says why; --quiesce=strict fails instead. Without --quiesce the set is crash-consistent within the spread, like a power cut of all members at once. The report and the web page show the point, the spread and the quiesce result. group sync --consistent takes the same kind of point without a rehearsal.

A group's settings live in its manifest; a single migration takes them as options (--access, --ssh-key, --ttl, --front-cidr, --host, and --tcp PORT or --http URL for its health check).

rehearsal:
  access: [203.0.113.0/24]          # who may SSH to the relay (the appliance always may)
  ssh_keys:                         # public keys of the relay's `rehearsal` user
    - ssh-ed25519 AAAA... alice@example.com
  hosts: {db.shop.internal: 10.20.0.31}   # names the relay's DNS answers
  front_cidr: 100.127.0.0/24        # the network standing in for the public interface
  ttl: 8h

docs.title: How the airgap is built
docs.text:
Risk What closes it A copy writes to production (same hostnames and addresses) The copies are created without a public interface (--public-ip none, set at creation on Exoscale) and attached only to isolated private networks created for the rehearsal, which hand out no router. There is no route to anything else Address conflicts The rehearsal networks are separate networks: the copies keep the production addresses (10.20.0.31 ...) without meeting production The relay as a way out The relay does not route: IP forwarding off, nftables forward policy drop, no NAT. Its sshd accepts keys only, and forwards (ssh -L, -W) only to the copies' addresses (PermitOpen); no tunnels, no gateway ports, no agent forwarding Who reaches the relay Its security group: SSH from the appliance and the access addresses only DNS The rehearsal networks hand out the relay as DNS server; it also answers on the on-premises DNS addresses the guests have configured, when they fall inside a rehearsal network. It answers the names in hosts, refuses everything else at once, and logs every query Replication Untouched: the copies come from Block Storage snapshots of the replicas and from one read of each replica's root disk (through its boot mask), while that migration's lock is held (minutes). The next sync is an ordinary delta. A production receiver, which allows no egress, may open SSH to the relay for that read; destroy closes it again The sources Never touched: the copies come from Exoscale, not from vSphere

Before any copy boots its converted system, exo-v2v checks through the API that no copy has a public IP or any other network, that the rehearsal networks hand out no router, and that the relay's forwarding is off.

In our lab, a 5-VM application (HAProxy, two application servers, PostgreSQL, a Windows Server member) ran as copies while production kept writing two rows a second to its own database: the copies wrote theirs into the copied database only, and the production rate did not change. From inside a copy: no default route; the internet, the appliance and the on-premises networks unreachable, even with a default route set by hand towards the relay; a DNS lookup refused in 13 ms; ssh -W through the relay to an address other than a copy refused.

docs.title: The sequence
docs.text:
1. Preflight: every member synced, receiver templates present, quotas.
  2. Networks: the front network (DHCP, front_cidr) and a copy of every private network the members use, same CIDR, the relay as DNS server.
  3. Relay: a small Debian instance (standard.small) with a public IP and a NIC on every rehearsal network.
  4. Copies' receivers: the exo-v2v receiver template, no public IP, on the front network, then on the private networks with the members' addresses (static leases). The appliance drives them through the relay.
  5. Airgap check (above).
  6. Seed, per member, its migration's lock held: snapshots of the production volumes become the copy's volumes (seconds); the production receiver streams its root disk to the copy through the relay (zero blocks skipped: a 40 GB disk with 5 GB of data took 31 s).
  7. Convert all copies in parallel: virt-v2v-in-place, 4 KiB sector adaptation, volume rebuilds, the network fix-up for the copy's NICs.
  8. Start, back to front, with the health checks on the relay; a failed check is reported, the rest keeps running.
  9. Report. The copies stay up until destroy or the TTL.

Every step is recorded: after an interruption, run the same command again.

docs.title: Requirements and limits
docs.text:
• Receiver templates built with exo-v2v 0.4 or later: an instance without a public IP gets its metadata from a read-only drive, not from the metadata server, and only these templates read it. A rehearsal cannot use the stock-template receiver (it installs packages from the internet).
  • Each copy is crash-consistent at its own seed time; members seeded minutes apart are not consistent with one another at one instant, unless you use --consistent (above).
  • Not rehearsed: what needs the public side (public IP, Elastic IPs and DNS switch, security groups on the public interface) and anything that needs the internet or your on-premises systems (they fail by design; the DNS log shows what was tried).
  • Windows copies: the replica of a running Windows has an unclean NTFS journal, which the conversion cannot mount read-write. On the copy only, exo-v2v resets the system disk's journal (ntfsfix -d) before converting and marks the volume for a check afterwards: Windows runs chkdsk at the copy's first boot, and changes in flight at the seed moment may be missing on the copy. (A real cutover shuts Windows down first: its disks are clean.)
  • Windows copies cannot reach activation or domain servers unless those are members of the group.
  • The copies see a small extra disk (the 1 MiB metadata drive), as the second disk: a Linux guest that mounts a data disk by device name (/dev/vdb) rather than by UUID or label finds the wrong disk there. Mounts by UUID (the usual case) are not affected.
  • Cost: a rehearsal adds one instance per copy (the target type, after conversion at standard.large), their volumes, and the relay, for its lifetime. group cutover refuses to start while a rehearsal of the group is up (--allow-rehearsal overrides).

docs.title: Project status
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

exo-v2v is labelled experimental: it works end to end in our lab, but it has not yet moved anyone's production. This page says what was tested, what was not, and what it takes to drop the label.

docs.title: Tested
docs.text: Area How Source Standalone ESXi 7.0 Update 3, VMFS datastore on HDDs, one replication appliance (4 vCPU) Target Exoscale ch-gva-2, receiver templates and stock templates Guests Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, AlmaLinux 9, Windows Server 2022 and 2025, BIOS and UEFI (details); LVM across disks, VMDK snapshot chains, 512-byte-sector XFS, NTFS data volumes Single VMs Plan, replication while the VM runs, cutover, rollback, cleanup; disks that grow or appear during replication Groups A 5-VM application (load balancer, two application servers, PostgreSQL, Windows) cut over, rolled back, killed and resumed; private networks with the VMs' addresses; 10 VMs on 18 disks (55 GB) replicated by one appliance and cut over in one 803-second window, with a rehearsal of 8 of them Rehearsals Airgapped copies of the 5-VM application and of single VMs, followed by real cutovers Safety Target instances restarted mid-replication (BIOS, UEFI, Windows): nothing boots, recover copies the system disk only; targets created by 0.4.0 upgraded in place vCenter Inventory paths, duplicate names, folders, tags, the privilege check and DRS settings, against govmomi's vCenter simulator (in CI) Unattended systemd timers, webhook alerts for failing and lagging replication, a target that went down, cutovers Public side A 5-VM application cut over with Elastic IPs on a Debian load balancer and a Windows server (both answering on them), a reverse DNS name, two members renumbered (Ubuntu netplan, Windows), a security group rule with a group as source; two Exoscale DNS records switched once it was healthy (served by every nameserver within 7 s), put back by the rollback, TTLs restored by the cleanup; the same for a single VM; rolled back, Elastic IPs released WAN One limit shared by concurrent copies (within 1 % of 160 Mbit/s), a limit change applied within 20 s in the middle of a copy, zlib compression (an Ubuntu disk to 38 %, Windows to 51 %), a cutover under a limit, a 40-minute copy (the vSphere session kept alive) Upgrades A target created by 0.5.0 cut over by 0.6.0 (plain writes), and one upgraded in place by a 0.6.0 sync Consistent rehearsal 5 members snapshotted together and quiesced (VSS, fsfreeze) while the application wrote, all copies healthy Actions and MCP Web API jobs as systemd units, the refusals (no token, cutover, cross-site, busy), the MCP server over SSH CI Unit tests on Python 3.10, 3.12 and 3.13; the receiver's disk handling on loop devices; the simulator tests; a strict docs build

docs.title: Not tested yet
docs.text:
• A real vCenter: vMotion, Storage vMotion and DRS moves during a replication, privilege enforcement, vSAN and vVols datastores.
  • The 0.6 IAM rules (Elastic IPs, reverse DNS, DNS) under a restricted key.
  • ESXi 8 (our lab's CPU cannot run it), zones other than ch-gva-2.
  • Disks of several terabytes, and more than ten VMs in one group.
  • Encrypted disks, Windows dynamic disks and Storage Spaces on data disks (not supported, see Limitations).

docs.title: Dropping "experimental"
docs.text:
The label goes when all of these hold:

  1. A full run on a real vCenter cluster (DRS, shared datastores): plan, replication, a rehearsal, a group cutover, a rollback.
  2. Migrations outside our lab by at least one team, and their findings fixed.
  3. No open issue that can lose or corrupt data, or let a copy run next to its source (0.4.1 fixed the last one known: a target instance that restarted booted the replica on its disk).
  4. CI green on the release.

Found a problem, or ran exo-v2v somewhere new? Open an issue on GitHub.

docs.title: Supported operating systems
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

exo-v2v converts guests with virt-v2v-in-place, so it can migrate the guests virt-v2v supports. The tables below separate what we tested end to end from what we expect to work.

docs.title: Tested
docs.text:
Each guest below was migrated live from ESXi 7.0 Update 3 to Exoscale (zone ch-gva-2) while running, with a system disk and a separate data disk. After each migration we compared marker files on both disks with their checksums from the VMware build, and checked the boot, the network, the mounted data disk and the services.

Operating system BIOS UEFI Data disk Downtime Ubuntu 24.04 LTS Yes Yes Not checked: the test image's data disk was blank 2–3 min Debian 13 Yes Yes ext4 4–5 min AlmaLinux 9.8, SELinux enforcing Yes Yes XFS created with 512-byte sectors (rebuilt for 4 KiB sectors at cutover) 5–7 min Windows Server 2022 Yes Yes NTFS (adapted to 4 KiB sectors in place) 5–8 min Windows Server 2025 Yes Yes NTFS (adapted to 4 KiB sectors in place) 6–9 min

The downtime column covers every run. The chart shows the final run of each guest through a receiver template:

Ubuntu 24.04 and Windows Server 2022 were also migrated from UEFI with Secure Boot on: both booted on Exoscale with Secure Boot on (downtime 133 s and 455 s).

A Debian 13 VM under continuous write load was also migrated with a downtime of 5 minutes and no lost writes. Up to 8 migrations ran at the same time from one replication appliance. Every guest above was migrated with a receiver template; all except Windows Server 2025 also without one.

docs.title: Multi-disk VMs, LVM and VMDK chains
docs.text:
Two AlmaLinux 9 VMs (SELinux enforcing, XFS with 512-byte sectors, the RHEL default on VMware) were migrated live with cutover --verify (every disk hash-compared before conversion):

VM What it had Result 4 disks on 3 controllers (2 paravirtual SCSI, NVMe) Root volume group on the system disk; XFS data disk; a volume group over a GPT partition of one disk and the whole NVMe disk, with an XFS logical volume spanning both and an ext4 one Pass: the XFS data disk and the spanning logical volume rebuilt with 4 KiB sectors (across two new volumes, same LVM and filesystem UUIDs), every file intact Root volume group extended onto a second disk, data disk grown before the migration Replication through a 3-level snapshot chain, then between cycles: a middle snapshot deleted, a revert to a snapshot, the data disk grown, the system disk grown, a disk hot-added Pass: the second disk carried inside the root disk; the revert copied the allocated areas again (the reverted file is absent, the later ones present); the data volume resized; the receiver reset with a bigger root disk; a volume added for the new disk

docs.title: An application moved as a group
docs.text:
A 5-VM application was moved with exo-v2v group (tiers, private network with the VMs' static addresses, health checks), three times:

VM Guest Network configuration on VMware Result Load balancer Debian 13, HAProxy ifupdown, a DHCP front NIC and a static back NIC Front NIC on the public interface, back NIC on the private network with its address 2 application servers AlmaLinux 9 (NetworkManager, eth0 naming), Ubuntu 24.04 (netplan) Static address, default route via the on-premises gateway Address kept on the private network, default route moved to the public interface Database AlmaLinux 9, PostgreSQL on an XFS data disk with 512-byte sectors Static address Same; data disk rebuilt for 4 KiB sectors, every row present Windows member Windows Server 2022 Static address Address set on the private network adapter at first boot

Window (first VM stopped to last tier healthy): 461 s for 4 VMs, 486 s for 5. A conversion failure injected on one member stopped the group, and group rollback brought the application back on VMware without losing data.

A Windows Server 2022 VM with a spanned dynamic volume over two disks lost that volume on Exoscale, as expected (see Limitations); its basic C: and D: volumes migrated fine. exo-v2v now reports dynamic disks before the cutover.

docs.title: Expected to work
docs.text:
These are supported by virt-v2v and use the same mechanisms as the tested guests, but we have not migrated them in our lab. Migrate a non-critical VM first.

Family Versions Red Hat Enterprise Linux and rebuilds (Rocky Linux, AlmaLinux, Oracle Linux, CentOS Stream) 8, 9, 10 Debian 11, 12 Ubuntu LTS 20.04, 22.04 SUSE Linux Enterprise Server, openSUSE Leap 15 Windows Server 2016, 2019

Older releases (for example RHEL 7 or Windows Server 2012 R2) may convert but are out of their vendors' support; we do not recommend them.

docs.title: Not supported
docs.text: Case Why Windows client editions (Windows 10, 11) Not tested; out of scope for this release Encrypted system disks (LUKS, BitLocker) The conversion has to read and modify the guest's system disk Operating systems other than Linux and Windows (FreeBSD, Solaris, …) virt-v2v does not convert them 32-bit guests Not tested; Exoscale instances are 64-bit VMs with more than 5 data disks (unless carried inside the root disk), independent disks or raw device mappings See Limitations Windows dynamic disks and Storage Spaces as data disks Their metadata counts 512-byte sectors; see Limitations

docs.title: Windows licensing
docs.text: A migrated Windows Server runs on an instance created from a Linux template, unless its receiver template is a Windows-licensed one published by Exoscale (not available yet, see Receiver templates). Contact Exoscale before migrating Windows workloads to agree on licensing.

docs.title: vCenter
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

exo-v2v talks to a vCenter Server the way it talks to a standalone ESXi host: VSPHERE_HOST names the vCenter (vcenter.example.com, or vcenter.example.com:8443 on another port), VSPHERE_USER an SSO account with the role below. This page covers what a vCenter adds: several datacenters and clusters, folders and tags, roles, DRS.

What was tested. Everything that reads or writes disks was validated on a standalone ESXi 7.0 U3. The vCenter code paths (inventory paths, duplicate names, folders, tags, the privilege check, DRS settings) are tested against govmomi's vCenter simulator (vcsim), in CI. vMotion, Storage vMotion and DRS moves during a replication, and privilege enforcement by a real vCenter, are not tested yet.

docs.title: Naming the VMs
docs.text:
Form Example When Name --vm web01 The name is unique in the vCenter (templates do not count) Inventory path --vm DC1/vm/shop/web01 Several VMs share the name (two datacenters, two folders): exo-v2v refuses the bare name and lists their paths Instance UUID --vm uuid:5032c8a4-... Scripts

A migration records the VM's instance UUID: renaming the VM or moving it to another folder afterwards does not lose it.

For a group, group discover takes VMs by name or path, a whole folder, or a vCenter tag, in any mix:

exo-v2v group discover shop --folder DC1/vm/shop --zone ch-gva-2
exo-v2v group discover shop --tag app:shop --vm DC1/vm/infra/lb01 --zone ch-gva-2

--folder includes subfolders. --tag CATEGORY:TAG reads the vSphere Automation API (/api, or /rest on vCenter 6.7 and early 7.0); standalone ESXi hosts have no tags. The draft manifest names each VM by its name, or by its path when the name is ambiguous.

docs.title: The vCenter role
docs.text:
Create a role with these privileges and grant it to the migration account:

Where Privileges The source VMs (or their folder, with propagation) VirtualMachine.State.CreateSnapshot, VirtualMachine.State.RemoveSnapshot, VirtualMachine.Config.ChangeTracking, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOff, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOn, VirtualMachine.Provisioning.DiskRandomRead The replication appliance VM VirtualMachine.Config.AddExistingDisk, VirtualMachine.Config.RemoveDisk The source VMs' datastores Datastore.FileManagement

With govc:

govc role.create exo-v2v VirtualMachine.State.CreateSnapshot VirtualMachine.State.RemoveSnapshot \
  VirtualMachine.Config.ChangeTracking VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOff VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOn \
  VirtualMachine.Provisioning.DiskRandomRead VirtualMachine.Config.AddExistingDisk \
  VirtualMachine.Config.RemoveDisk Datastore.FileManagement
govc permissions.set -principal exo-v2v@vsphere.local -role exo-v2v -propagate=true /DC1/vm/shop
govc permissions.set -principal exo-v2v@vsphere.local -role exo-v2v -propagate=false /DC1/vm/infra/v2v-appliance
govc permissions.set -principal exo-v2v@vsphere.local -role exo-v2v -propagate=false /DC1/datastore/ds-prod-01

With PowerCLI:

$p = Get-VIPrivilege -Id VirtualMachine.State.CreateSnapshot, VirtualMachine.State.RemoveSnapshot,
  VirtualMachine.Config.ChangeTracking, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOff, VirtualMachine.Interact.PowerOn,
  VirtualMachine.Provisioning.DiskRandomRead, VirtualMachine.Config.AddExistingDisk,
  VirtualMachine.Config.RemoveDisk, Datastore.FileManagement
New-VIRole -Name exo-v2v -Privilege $p
New-VIPermission -Entity (Get-Folder shop) -Principal 'VSPHERE.LOCAL\exo-v2v' -Role exo-v2v -Propagate:$true
New-VIPermission -Entity (Get-VM v2v-appliance) -Principal 'VSPHERE.LOCAL\exo-v2v' -Role exo-v2v
New-VIPermission -Entity (Get-Datastore ds-prod-01) -Principal 'VSPHERE.LOCAL\exo-v2v' -Role exo-v2v

exo-v2v plan (and group plan) asks the vCenter which of these privileges the account lacks on the VM, its datastores and, when it runs on the appliance as root, the appliance VM, and lists them as warnings.

docs.title: Where the appliance runs
docs.text:
The appliance reads a VM's disks by attaching its frozen snapshot disks to itself (hot-add), so its host must mount every datastore of the VMs it replicates. In a cluster with shared datastores, any host will do; VMs on a host's local datastore need an appliance on that host. plan (run on the appliance) warns when its host does not see a datastore of the VM; sync refuses to start, naming the datastore.

DRS must not move the appliance while snapshot disks are attached to it. In a cluster with fully automated DRS, plan and sync warn until the appliance has a VM override (DRS automation level Disabled, or Partially automated).

docs.title: During the replication
docs.text: Event Effect The source VM moves to another host (vMotion, DRS) Nothing: snapshots and hot-add do not depend on the VM's host. Each cycle checks again that the appliance's host sees the VM's datastores The source VM's disks move (Storage vMotion) Each cycle reads the disk paths again. When VMware resets the change tracking, the next cycle copies the allocated areas of the disks again (a full cycle, not a broken one). A cycle running while a disk moves fails and the next one starts over The VM is renamed or moved to another folder Nothing: the migration finds it by instance UUID

docs.title: Web status page
docs.text:
Experimental. exo-v2v 0.6.0 is an early release, validated in one lab (ESXi 7.0 U3 to Exoscale ch-gva-2). Try it on non-critical VMs first; commands and behaviour may change.

exo-v2v web serves a page with the state of every migration and group on the replication appliance: phases, the last cycles, cutover steps, downtime, member logs. Share it with the people who follow a migration without giving them a shell. It is read-only unless you enable actions (a sync cycle, a rehearsal, destroying a rehearsal; never a cutover or a rollback).

sudo -E exo-v2v web                      # http://127.0.0.1:8780/

Run it as the user that runs the migrations (sudo -E, the same EXO_V2V_HOME): it reads their state files.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Page Content Overview Groups (cutover state, members by tier and phase), every migration: phase, a sync or cutover running now, a receiver down, failed cycles in a row (the last error on hover), last cycle (highlighted when older than the lag alert threshold), public and private addresses, downtime; the WAN limit now; recent jobs Migration Phase, source VM, receiver, Elastic IP and DNS records, a chart of the data copied per cycle (full, delta, final), the bytes sent per cycle (after compression, with the time spent waiting for the WAN limit), disks and where they go, networks with the Exoscale MACs, the cutover steps with their times, plan and preflight messages, events, jobs Job The command, who started it, its state and log; a button to interrupt it Rehearsal Its copies (phase, address, seed and boot times, health from the relay), its steps, networks, the names the copies tried to resolve, the TTL Group Members by tier with their health check results, the cutover steps (preflight, warm cycle, tiers off, conversions, tiers up, hooks) with their times, networks, a member's log, events

The page refreshes every 5 seconds. It needs no internet access: no external scripts, fonts or images.

docs.title: Read-only (by default)
docs.text:
• Reading never writes a file and never takes a lock: a running sync or cutover is found from the process ID its lock file records.
  • Writes exist only for actions: off unless actions: enabled: true in config.yaml and the server has a token (on loopback too). Any other write gets 405.
  • It needs no Exoscale or vSphere credentials, and serves no keys: the migration's SSH key and the tunnel's known_hosts are not exposed. Logs are served only for group members, by name.

docs.title: Access
docs.text:
It listens on 127.0.0.1:8780 by default. From your workstation:

ssh -L 8780:127.0.0.1:8780 appliance      # then open http://127.0.0.1:8780/

Without a token, it answers only requests addressed to 127.0.0.1 or localhost (a web page elsewhere cannot reach it through a DNS name that resolves to 127.0.0.1). To listen on another address, set a token; the page refuses to start without one:

openssl rand -hex 24 | sudo tee /etc/exo-v2v-web.token >/dev/null
sudo -E exo-v2v web --listen 0.0.0.0:8780 --token-file /etc/exo-v2v-web.token

The page asks for the token once and keeps it in an HTTP-only cookie (/login?token=TOKEN still works, but leaves the token in the browser's history). API clients send Authorization: Bearer TOKEN. The page is plain HTTP: put it behind a TLS reverse proxy, or keep the SSH tunnel, on any network you do not trust. EXO_V2V_WEB_TOKEN can carry the token instead of a file.

docs.title: Run it as a service
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/exo-v2v-web.service
[Unit]
Description=exo-v2v read-only status page
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Environment=EXO_V2V_HOME=/var/lib/exo-v2v
ExecStart=/opt/exo-v2v/bin/exo-v2v web --listen 127.0.0.1:8780
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
